content: 1. There are gaps in national tuberculosis (TB) case detection efforts, which need to be addressed. This includes analyzing whether these gaps are due to under-diagnosis, under-notification, or both. Data from previous epidemiological reviews and health system assessments can be utilized for this purpose. 2. Major initiatives involving private providers, such as Public-Private Mix (PPM) models or insurance schemes, should be reviewed. Published success stories and program review reports can serve as valuable data sources. The assessment should also examine private sector engagement in other vertical health programs (e.g., HIV, malaria, family planning, maternal and child health) to identify opportunities for integration with TB efforts. 3. The proportion of TB notifications originating from different sources, such as public hospitals, private hospitals, and other providers, should be determined. 4. The causes and average duration of delays in TB diagnosis should be analyzed to identify barriers to timely care. 5. Data on the availability and sales volumes of TB drugs in the private sector, if available, should be reviewed to understand market dynamics. 6. Patterns of health-seeking behavior among individuals with TB symptoms should be studied. This includes identifying the types of providers they first approach and mapping their pathways to quality TB diagnosis and treatment. Such data can be sourced from patient pathway analyses and TB prevalence surveys. 7. The number and types of providers engaged in TB care, including public hospitals, private hospitals, specialists (e.g., pulmonologists, pediatricians), general practitioners, pharmacists, laboratories, informal providers, and workplace health facilities, should be documented. This should also include facilities overseen by other ministries, such as those in prisons or the armed forces. 8. The number of providers already contributing to quality TB diagnosis, treatment, and notifications to the National TB Program should be identified. 9. The mechanisms and outcomes of PPM engagement models in the country should be evaluated. This includes methods for provider engagement, education, monitoring, and support, as well as the financial and personnel requirements for each model. The referral, case detection, and treatment success rates of these models should also be assessed. 10. Current funding sources and amounts for TB PPM, including national and donor contributions, should be identified. 11. Existing mechanisms for collecting data on private provider numbers, their engagement with the TB program, and their contributions to TB notifications should be reviewed. This includes assessing the use or development of mHealth applications. 12. Major professional associations in the country should be identified, along with indicators of their institutional capacity (e.g., annual budget, number of paid staff, membership size) and their involvement in TB PPM activities. 13. The current regulatory environment should be assessed, including provider licensing, facility accreditation, mandatory TB notification, and the regulation of antibiotic dispensing (specifically TB drugs). The extent of enforcement and the mechanisms used for enforcement should also be evaluated. 14. PPM-related actions and operational gaps identified in the National TB Strategic Plan (NSP) should be reviewed. 15. The status of universal health coverage (UHC) and social protection schemes for TB patients in the country should be assessed, including considerations for covering private patients under these schemes. 16. Field visits and consultations should be planned to gather detailed information and ensure interactions with diverse stakeholders, including public and private managers and implementers at all levels of the health system. 17. A national PPM action plan should define a clear goal, strategic objectives, and a timeline, typically covering a five-year period. Specific sub-objectives and activities should be outlined under each strategic objective. 18. The task mix for TB care and prevention should be defined, specifying the roles of different provider types. This should include referral pathways and the potential role of intermediary agencies in facilitating PPM efforts. 19. Monitoring and evaluation systems for PPM should be established, including methods for summarizing and analyzing data at different levels of the health system. 20. Strategies for increasing domestic and donor financing for PPM should be developed. This includes integrating TB into insurance initiatives and using reimbursements to engage more private providers in quality TB care. 21. All activities and targets should be specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound (SMART). A log frame should be developed to outline strategic objectives, sub-objectives, activities, timelines, responsible organizations, funders, and targets for each year of the action plan. 22. Capacity-building efforts should focus on pre-service and in-service training for providers, as well as institutional capacity building for organizations delivering PPM services. Local PPM leadership groups should also be supported to create localized roadmaps for PPM implementation. 23. The consultation group should discuss necessary actions, whether detailed assessments or immediate rollouts of existing models are required, and the human and financial resources needed for implementation. Each major area of work should have a designated organization responsible for its execution.
